source: Text and transliteration: Rekhta, via github.com/amir9ume/urdu_ghazals_rekhta
summary: The ghazal reflects on intense longing, love, disgrace, and fate, with the refrain 'nikle' repeatedly marking what emerges or results from desire, cruelty, or circumstance. Ghalib moves from unfulfilled wishes and the lover's humiliation to ironic contrasts with Adam's expulsion, the beloved's beauty, wine-drinking, and the preacher's hypocrisy. The overall mood is one of wounded pride and paradox, where love erases the difference between living and dying.

ur: ہزاروں خواہشیں ایسی کہ ہر خواہش پہ دم نکلے
بہت نکلے مرے ارمان لیکن پھر بھی کم نکلے
roman: hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ aisī ki har ḳhvāhish pe dam nikle
bahut nikle mire armān lekin phir bhī kam nikle

phrases.gloss: breath may pass; one may die

poetic: Thousands of desires, each one such that a life could end upon it;
Many of my longings came to pass, yet still they were too few.
notes: The phrase dam nikalna means to die or to have ones breath depart; here each desire is felt so intensely that it could kill.
The verb nikalna is repeated at the end of both lines: first for death from desire, then for longings emerging or being fulfilled.
Arman can mean unfulfilled wishes, regrets, or longings; the speaker says many came out, yet they still seem far too few.
The first line sets up a hyperbolic result clause with ki: such desires that every single desire would make life leave.
The couplet turns on the paradox of insatiable desire: even many fulfilled longings are less than the thousands the heart holds.

ur: ڈرے کیوں میرا قاتل کیا رہے گا اس کی گردن پر
وہ خوں جو چشم تر سے عمر بھر یوں دم بدم نکلے
roman: Dare kyuuñ merā qātil kyā rahegā us kī gardan par
vo ḳhuuñ jo chashm-e-tar se umr bhar yuuñ dam-ba-dam nikle

phrases.gloss: flowed out continually, moment by moment

poetic: Why should my killer fear? What blood could stay upon his neck,
when from my weeping eyes it flowed out moment by moment all my life?
notes: The lover's tears of blood are a metaphor for his lifeblood draining away through grief; the beloved's 'killing' is thus bloodless.
The rhetorical question 'What blood will remain on his neck?' implies the beloved can shed no actual blood because the lover has already wept it all out.
'Dam-ba-dam' literally means 'breath by breath' but implies continuous, unceasing action, linking weeping and dying.
'Chashm-e-tar' is a Persian izafat compound: 'tar' means moist or wet, so the compound means 'wet eye'—here tears of blood.
The couplet plays on the idea of blood-guilt: if no blood remains, the beloved killer has nothing to fear, yet the lover's whole life has been one long bleeding.

ur: نکلنا خلد سے آدم کا سنتے آئے ہیں لیکن
بہت بے آبرو ہو کر ترے کوچے سے ہم نکلے
roman: nikalnā ḳhuld se aadam kā sunte aa.e haiñ lekin
bahut be-ābrū ho kar tire kūche se ham nikle

units.base: to come out, to go out

poetic: We have heard of Adam's going out from Eden—true;
but from your lane we came forth far more dishonoured too.
notes: The verse contrasts Adam's expulsion from Paradise with the lover's departure from the beloved's lane, claiming the lover's disgrace is even greater.
Khuld refers to Paradise or the Garden of Eden, while the beloved's lane, kūcha, is the earthly site of the lover's longing and public humiliation.
Be-ābrū literally means without water of the face, meaning dishonoured or disgraced; ābrū combines āb, water, and rū, face.
Sunte āe haiñ means they have always heard or have heard from long-standing tradition, setting scriptural report against personal experience.
The repetition of nikalnā and nikle underlines the parallel between Adam's expulsion and the speaker's exit.

ur: بھرم کھل جائے ظالم تیرے قامت کی درازی کا
اگر اس طرۂ پر پیچ و خم کا پیچ و خم نکلے
roman: bharam khul jaa.e zālim tere qāmat kī darāzī kā
agar is turra-e-pur-pech-o-ḳham kā pech-o-ḳham nikle

units.gloss: the forelock full of twists and curls

poetic: O cruel one, the illusion of your tallness would be exposed
if the twists and curls of that twist-and-curl-filled forelock were unrolled.
notes: bharam khulnā is an idiom meaning 'the secret/illusion is revealed'.
The beloved's tall stature is imagined as an illusion created by the high, curled forelock; if its curls were straightened, the height would vanish.
The repetition of pech-o-kham—first as adjective pur-pech-o-kham ('full of twists and curls') and then as noun pech-o-kham ('twists and curls')—creates a wordplay on the same root.
zālim (cruel one) is a conventional address to the beloved in Urdu ghazal, not a literal accusation.
The conditional agar... nikle (if... would come out) sets a hypothetical, almost impossible condition.

ur: مگر لکھوائے کوئی اس کو خط تو ہم سے لکھوائے
ہوئی صبح اور گھر سے کان پر رکھ کر قلم نکلے
roman: magar likhvā.e koī us ko ḳhat to ham se likhvā.e
huī sub.h aur ghar se kaan par rakh kar qalam nikle

literal.text: should someone have a letter written to him

poetic: But if anyone would have a letter written to him, then let it be written by me;
day broke, and from his house he came out with a pen placed on his ear.
notes: The repeated likhvā.e is the causative of likhnā, meaning to get something written; the line shifts the writing to the poet himself.
Putting a pen on the ear is a traditional gesture of a scribe or schoolboy, making the beloved look ready to write.
There is gentle irony: though the beloved appears with a pen on his ear, the poet claims that any letter-writing should be done by him.
The phrase sub.h huī is an idiom for daybreak, literally meaning 'morning became'.
The poetic plural ham is used for the singular first person, giving the speaker a formal or self-effacing tone.

ur: ہوئی اس دور میں منسوب مجھ سے بادہ آشامی
پھر آیا وہ زمانہ جو جہاں میں جام جم نکلے
roman: huī is daur meñ mansūb mujh se bāda-ashāmī
phir aayā vo zamāna jo jahāñ meñ jām-e-jam nikle
poetic: In this age, wine-drinking has been pinned on me—
that age has come again when Jamshid’s cup appears in the world.
notes: jām-e-jam is the legendary Cup of Jamshid, a Persian kingly goblet that revealed the world; here it also puns on an actual wine cup.
bāda-ashāmī is a formal Persian compound meaning wine-drinking or wine-bibbing, used almost as an accusation or title.
The verse ironically turns the speaker’s reputation for drinking into proof that a mythic, glorious age has returned.

ur: ہوئی جن سے توقع خستگی کی داد پانے کی
وہ ہم سے بھی زیادہ خستۂ تیغ ستم نکلے
roman: huī jin se tavaqqo ḳhastagī kī daad paane kī
vo ham se bhī ziyāda ḳhasta-e-teġh-e-sitam nikle

units.gloss: wounded by the sword of cruelty

literal.text: wounded by the sword of cruelty

poetic: Those from whom I hoped to receive sympathy for my woundedness—
they turned out even more wounded by the sword of cruelty than I.
notes: The phrase 'daad paana' means to receive sympathy, appreciation, or justice; 'daad' in classical Urdu often means praise or consolation for one's pain or art.
The same root 'khasta' is repeated in 'khastagī' and 'khasta-e-tegh-e-sitam', turning the speaker's woundedness back onto those from whom he expected sympathy.
'Tegh-e-sitam' (sword of cruelty) is a standard metaphor for the beloved's tyranny or the cruelty of fate.
The comparison 'ham se bhī ziyāda' creates an ironic reversal: the people he looked to for consolation prove even more afflicted than he is.
'Nikle' carries the sense of 'turned out' or 'proved to be', revealing the true state of those people.

ur: محبت میں نہیں ہے فرق جینے اور مرنے کا
اسی کو دیکھ کر جیتے ہیں جس کافر پہ دم نکلے
roman: mohabbat meñ nahīñ hai farq jiine aur marne kā
usī ko dekh kar jiite haiñ jis kāfir pe dam nikle

phrases.gloss: to die; to expire; breath leaves the body

literal.text: In love there is no difference of living and dying
By seeing that very one we live:

poetic: In love, living and dying are one:
we live by seeing that very infidel at whose sight the breath expires.
notes: The couplet turns on the paradox that in love, life and death are indistinguishable.
dam nikalnā is an idiom meaning to die or to expire.
kāfir here is the beloved, not a religious unbeliever; in ghazal convention the beloved is often a beautiful infidel or cruel idol.
The lover lives only through the sight of the beloved, yet that same sight makes the breath depart.
The relative jis kāfir refers back to usī in the first half, binding the whole couplet around a single shocking figure.

ur: کہاں مے خانہ کا دروازہ غالبؔ اور کہاں واعظ
پر اتنا جانتے ہیں کل وہ جاتا تھا کہ ہم نکلے
roman: kahāñ mai-ḳhāne kā darvāza 'ġhālib' aur kahāñ vaa.iz
par itnā jānte haiñ kal vo jaatā thā ki ham nikle

phrases.gloss: where X and where Y (idiom of vast difference, no comparison)

poetic: Where stands the tavern door, Ghalib—and where the preacher?
Yet this I know: he was heading in as I came out yesterday.
notes: The pattern 'kahāñ ... aur kahāñ' expresses enormous separation or total lack of comparison between two things.
The preacher is a stock figure of outward piety, so his appearing at the tavern door hints at hypocrisy.
The tavern door is a symbolic threshold of forbidden pleasure, contrasted with the preacher's public morality.
The word 'kal' can mean yesterday or tomorrow, but the past auxiliary 'thā' fixes it here as yesterday.
The line suggests a simultaneous encounter at the threshold: the preacher enters as the poet or speaker leaves.
